ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy is the gold standard for synaptic maps, but for most groups it remains prohibitively costly in imaging time, data storage, and analysis. A cheaper multi-resolution path would let small labs do comparative circuit work without full-brain synaptic volumes.
ocar.challenge: Global projectomes at cellular resolution and local synaptic connectomes pull in opposite directions on cost and throughput. Automated segmentation also fails where membranes have holes, and synapse prediction quality drops as image quality falls from best to moderate.
ocar.action: Gillet, Sayre, Badalamente, Schieber, Tedore, Funke, and Heinze present on bioRxiv (2026) a standardized pipeline for volume-EM preparation, acquisition, and alignment, combined with µCT block trimming, automatic segmentation, synapse detection, CATMAID skeleton tracing, and CAVE proofreading, applied to the central complex of six insect species.
ocar.resolution: The pipeline yielded global projectomes at 40–50 nm with embedded local connectomes of key computational compartments at 8–12 nm. Reconstructing head-direction cells across all six species showed conserved cell types, cell numbers, and projection patterns plus circuit-level specializations. The authors argue this makes comparative connectomics accessible to groups with modest resources.
ocar.future_work: Corrective splits in CAVE were still required where membrane holes caused false merges, and synapse F-scores in Megalopta genalis varied with image quality, so applying the same modest-resource workflow to other neuropils will depend on keeping acquisition in the high-quality regime.

summaries.beginner: Mapping insect brains is usually too expensive for small labs. This team images the same brain at two zoom levels and finds that a navigation circuit looks largely the same across six insect species, with some local tweaks.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), Gillet and colleagues describe a multi-resolution volume-EM pipeline aimed at groups with modest resources. Applied to the central complex of six insect species, it produced cellular-resolution global projectomes (40–50 nm) with embedded local connectomes at synaptic resolution (8–12 nm), using CATMAID tracing and CAVE proofreading alongside automated segmentation and synapse detection. Reconstructing head-direction (EPG/PEG) cells across species revealed conservation of cell types, numbers, and projection patterns together with circuit-level specializations. Figure supplements document remaining reconstruction issues: membrane holes that cause false merges and synapse-prediction F-scores that decline as image quality falls.
summaries.advanced: The “democratizing” claim rests on a six-species central-complex case study rather than a full-brain reconstruction. Conservation is reported for head-direction cells specifically. F-scores are shown for Megalopta genalis neuropils (PB, FB, NO) across image-quality bins, not as a single pipeline-wide accuracy. The extract does not quantify wall-clock cost or tracing completeness. Novelty is in integration and multi-resolution strategy more than in a single new algorithm.

plain_language_summary: Mapping insect brains is usually too expensive for small labs. This team images the same brain at two zoom levels and finds that a navigation circuit looks largely the same across six insect species, with some local tweaks.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric EM now yields terabyte-to-petabyte datasets, but automated synapse detectors still depend on scarce expert labels. Crowdsourcing could supply that supervision if noisy human judgments can be turned into auditable consensus.
ocar.challenge: Synapse identification hinges on subtle 3D cues, so raters disagree, and chance-corrected agreement metrics such as Krippendorff’s α are depressed by even a single dissenting score. The study was limited to two larval Drosophila sub-volumes and a small rater cohort.
ocar.action: Lee, Correia, Ceffa, Robbins, Franco-Barranco, Zlatic, Cardona, and Mohinta present on bioRxiv (2026) a standardized proofreading protocol that pairs operational criteria with machine-learning candidate generation, two-stage annotator calibration, and Dawid–Skene aggregation of five raters (one expert plus four calibrated annotators) on model-proposed candidates in two larval Drosophila volumes imaged at 8×8×8 nm.
ocar.resolution: Post-calibration, each annotator’s accuracy versus the expert improved (McNemar p < 0.05 for all raters), Dawid–Skene–expert agreement rose, and posterior entropy fell for true positives and negatives. Gains in Krippendorff’s α were modest and dataset-dependent. The protocol converts multi-rater judgments into consensus labels with calibrated uncertainty.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag extensions in scale and diversity (more raters and volumes), generalization across organisms and modalities, and unbiased sampling to mitigate selection effects. Near-term they advocate using Dawid–Skene entropy to prioritize reviews, stratifying tasks by difficulty, and training detectors on soft consensus labels rather than hard labels alone.

summaries.beginner: People often disagree about whether a tiny blob in a brain image is a synapse. This team trains raters, combines their votes with a statistical model, and reports how sure the group is, so the labels can be used more honestly.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), Lee and colleagues present a synapse-proofreading protocol for EM connectomics that pairs explicit criteria with model-proposed candidates and two-stage annotator calibration. In two larval Drosophila volumes at 8×8×8 nm, five raters labeled candidates, and judgments were aggregated with a Dawid–Skene model. After calibration, accuracy versus the expert improved for all raters (McNemar p < 0.05), consensus became more decisive, and residual uncertainty is retained rather than hidden. The conclusion section frames the output as auditable supervision for training and evaluation as datasets and teams scale.
summaries.advanced: The authors themselves limit the study to two larval Drosophila sub-volumes (MR and Octo) and a small rater cohort. Chance-corrected agreement gains were modest and dataset-dependent, so the protocol does not claim to eliminate rater noise. Evaluation is against a single expert. Future-work items (other organisms, unbiased sampling, soft labels) are proposed, not demonstrated here. Borderline cases remain the main source of residual ambiguity.

plain_language_summary: People often disagree about whether a tiny blob in a brain image is a synapse. This team trains raters, combines their votes with a statistical model, and reports how sure the group is, so the labels can be used more honestly.

ocar.opportunity: EM connectomics volumes are now so large and heterogeneous that manual annotation and dataset-specific retraining cannot keep up. A connectomics-specific foundation model could learn visual representations once and transfer them with little labeled data.
ocar.challenge: Recent EM foundation models provide general visual features but are not tailored to connectomics, where membrane boundaries and synaptic ultrastructure must be preserved to avoid topological and connectivity errors.
ocar.action: Abir, Saha, Naswan, and Bayzid introduce ConnectoFM on bioRxiv (2026): a model pretrained with masked image modeling and contrastive alignment on 1.7 million unlabeled EM images from six species and 25 subdomains, then transferred with frozen features and lightweight decoder heads to binary segmentation, multiclass cell typing, and instance segmentation.
ocar.resolution: Across 29 datasets, ConnectoFM outperformed existing EM foundation models and from-scratch task-specific methods. With 10% labeled data it surpassed baselines trained on a 100% annotation budget, with especially pronounced gains on membranes, mitochondria, vesicles, postsynaptic densities, and synapses. Representations clustered images by species, brain region, developmental cohort, and acquisition domain. The authors also report an extension to 3D volumetric segmentation.
ocar.future_work: The paper positions ConnectoFM as a scalable route toward more reliable circuit reconstruction; whether the same frozen features hold on acquisition domains outside the 25-subdomain corpus, and at full connectome-scale 3D volumes, is the implied next test.

summaries.beginner: Computers that trace neurons from electron-microscope pictures usually have to be retrained for every new dataset. This team pretrains one model on a huge mix of unlabeled brain images and shows it can learn new tracing jobs with far fewer hand-drawn labels.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), Abir and colleagues present ConnectoFM, described as a foundation model for connectomics, pretrained on 1.7 million unlabeled EM images from six species and 25 subdomains using masked image modeling plus contrastive alignment. Frozen features with light decoder heads transfer to binary segmentation, multiclass cell typing, and instance segmentation. Across 29 datasets the model outperforms existing EM foundation models and from-scratch specialists, and with 10% labels it beats baselines trained on 100% of the annotation budget. Gains are emphasized for membranes, mitochondria, vesicles, postsynaptic densities, and synapses, with a further extension to 3D volumetric segmentation.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s discussion was not captured (the selected PDF text runs into the reference list), so quantitative claims are those stated in the abstract and introduction. Competing foundation models are not named here, and per-dataset scores are not given. “First foundation model for connectomics” is an authorship claim. The 10%-versus-100% label result is striking and should be checked against the full tables. Introduction cites H01, MICrONS, and FlyWire as motivating large-scale targets rather than as evaluation volumes named in this extract.

plain_language_summary: Computers that trace neurons from electron-microscope pictures usually have to be retrained for every new dataset. This team pretrains one model on a huge mix of unlabeled brain images and shows it can learn new tracing jobs with far fewer hand-drawn labels.

ocar.opportunity: Generative models of cortical wiring usually start from measured features such as morphology, molecular identity, and location, so they can only use what we already know how to measure. Circuit structure may depend on features we cannot yet name.
ocar.challenge: Those assumed features may miss the variables that actually predict synapses, and neither superiority nor interpretability of purely connectivity-derived embeddings is guaranteed: prior knowledge can be a useful inductive bias.
ocar.action: Richter and Schneidman, on bioRxiv (2026), jointly learn low-dimensional neuronal embeddings and an artificial neural network of wiring rules that predict connection probabilities in a mouse primary visual cortex column from connectivity data alone, without feeding in a predefined biophysical feature set.
ocar.resolution: Embedding neurons in a 5-dimensional space and using 6 wiring rules accurately predicted individual connections, inter-layer connectivity, in- and out-degrees, and small motif distributions, outperforming standard generative models that depend on detailed cell-type classifications. Two dominant embedding axes corresponded to cortical depth and excitatory/inhibitory identity; a hybrid model using measured biological features plus 3 remaining abstract dimensions was on par with the original model.
ocar.future_work: The three abstract features that could not be explained in biological terms may point to unmeasured properties. The authors expect that more aligned connectivity and neuronal-characteristic data, in particular future transcriptomic data at the level of individual neurons, could map the latent space onto genetic and developmental interpretations.

summaries.beginner: Instead of starting from known cell labels, this study lets a model invent a compact description of each neuron and the simple rules that wire them together in mouse visual cortex. Two of those invented axes turn out to be depth and whether the cell is excitatory or inhibitory.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), Richter and Schneidman present a representational-learning model of a mouse primary visual cortex column. The framework jointly learns embeddings and wiring rules that predict synapses from connectivity alone. A 5-dimensional embedding with 6 rules predicted individual synapses, degrees, and motif statistics better than cell-type-based generative models. Two dominant features mapped to cortical depth and E/I identity; the remaining three were not explained by available measurements, though a hybrid model with those abstract dimensions plus biological features matched the original model. The authors argue that cortical connectivity follows a surprisingly parsimonious logic.
summaries.advanced: Success is reported for one cortical column. Three of five embedding dimensions remain unnamed, so interpretability is partial. The hybrid model being on par with the fully abstract model means known features plus leftover latents can substitute, not that a complete biological wiring table has been written. Motif and degree predictions are discussed qualitatively in the extract; numeric accuracies are not given here. Exportability to other areas and species is stated as a framework property, not a demonstrated transfer result.

plain_language_summary: Instead of starting from known cell labels, this study lets a model invent a compact description of each neuron and the simple rules that wire them together in mouse visual cortex. Two of those invented axes turn out to be depth and whether the cell is excitatory or inhibitory.

ocar.opportunity: Complete larval and adult Drosophila connectomes now make it possible to compare how an entire brain rewires across metamorphosis, not only how a few identified neurons change.
ocar.challenge: Larval and adult networks differ in density, cell composition, and which neurons sit at the structural core, and metamorphosis involves neuronal death, reorganization, and adult-specific neurons, so comparison requires matched network statistics rather than a cell-by-cell map.
ocar.action: Yadav, Shinde, and Singh, in Network Neuroscience (2025), compared degree distributions, modularity, D-core structural cores, and rich-club organization of Drosophila melanogaster brain networks at larval versus adult stages.
ocar.resolution: The denser larval network fitted a Weibull degree distribution (growth parameter β > 1); the sparser adult network followed a power law, with the out-degree exponent in the scale-free regime and the in-degree exponent close to it. Both networks were sparse and modular, but the adult was more modular. The larval D-core comprised mushroom-body neurons and formed a rich club; the adult core comprised antennal-lobe neurons, consistent with reduced mushroom-body centrality after metamorphosis.
ocar.future_work: The authors interpret the scale-free shift as an adaptation for robustness against failures while lowering density costs, and they contrast Drosophila’s metamorphic rewiring with C. elegans, whose degree distributions reportedly do not follow a power law across development. Linking these graph-level shifts to identified cell types and behaviors would test whether core relocation is a computational change.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly brains are rewired as the animal grows from larva to adult. This paper compares the two wiring diagrams and finds that the adult network is sparser and more hub-like, and that the most central cells change from a learning center to an odor center.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Network Neuroscience (2025), Yadav, Shinde, and Singh compare larval and adult Drosophila melanogaster brain networks. The larval degree distribution fitted a Weibull model, whereas the sparser adult network followed a power-law pattern. The adult brain is described as more modular, with more specialized compartments. Using D-core decomposition, the larval structural core comprised mushroom-body neurons and formed a rich club; the adult core comprised antennal-lobe neurons, and only the larva showed rich-club organization. The authors attribute the core shift to reduced mushroom-body centrality after metamorphosis.
summaries.advanced: Scale-free and Weibull fits are model comparisons on observed degree sequences; the adult in-degree “narrowly failing” the scale-free threshold is a borderline result. Some topological differences could follow from density reduction alone. Mapping mushroom-body versus antennal-lobe cores depends on how neurons are assigned to regions. The study compares two life stages of one species, not a time series of many individuals. The C. elegans contrast is cited from Zhao et al. (2022), not re-derived here.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly brains are rewired as the animal grows from larva to adult. This paper compares the two wiring diagrams and finds that the adult network is sparser and more hub-like, and that the most central cells change from a learning center to an odor center.

ocar.opportunity: The adult Drosophila connectome specifies synaptic paths that constrain how sensory signals can flow, but not how those paths unfold as dynamic cascades through higher-order structures such as the lateral horn, mushroom body, and central complex.
ocar.challenge: Sensory systems are initially segregated by modality, yet many functions require multi-step polysynaptic integration that is not obvious from first-order connectivity. Circuit-level mechanisms of multisensory integration remain poorly understood.
ocar.action: Betzel, Puxeddu, Seguin, and Mišić, on bioRxiv (2025), simulate sensory propagation on the adult Drosophila connectome with a network spreading model, extend it with cooperative and competitive dynamics, and classify neurons by dynamical response profiles across simulations.
ocar.resolution: The model produced modality-specific cascades and overlap zones of multi-pathway activation, plus a data-driven neuron taxonomy grounded in both structure and dynamics. Sensory neurons from different modalities were highly segregated, with minimal direct synaptic links. The authors highlight predicted co-activation of thermo- and hygrosensory pathways as a testable overlap.
ocar.future_work: They propose evaluating predicted multi-sensory hubs with paired or combinatorial stimulation, and enhancing the model with synaptic polarity, excitatory/inhibitory distinctions, and transmitter-specific dynamics. They also note that cascade-overlap measures require a neuron to be active in 25% of simulations, a threshold that could be informed by experimental evidence on what fraction of sensory neurons fire to a stimulus.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram shows which cells touch, not how a signal would actually travel. This team runs simple spreading simulations on the fly brain map to guess which cells light up together for different senses.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2025), Betzel and colleagues apply a cascade-style spreading model to the adult Drosophila connectome (described here as roughly 138,000–140,000 neurons). They trace modality-specific cascades, quantify overlap among sensory pathways, and add cooperative and competitive dynamics for multisensory integration. Neurons are then classified by response profiles across simulations. The discussion emphasizes that activation is passive and architecture-driven, and it offers the prediction that thermo- and hygrosensory pathways co-activate overlapping groups. Combining structure with stimulus-evoked recordings is proposed as a way to link wiring to function more directly.
summaries.advanced: The model abstracts away biophysics in favor of analytic clarity; the authors contrast it with integrate-and-fire realism. Synapse-count figures in the extract conflict (intro: 54 million synapses; discussion: over 15 million connections), so those totals should not be treated as a single authoritative count from this paper. The 25% activation criterion for overlap maps is a modeling choice. The taxonomy is simulation-derived and may not match molecular cell types. Validation against recordings is proposed, not performed here.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram shows which cells touch, not how a signal would actually travel. This team runs simple spreading simulations on the fly brain map to guess which cells light up together for different senses.

ocar.opportunity: Shared EM connectomes are now proofread and annotated by many users at once, and every edit can relabel millions of voxels and thousands of synapses. Collaboration needs infrastructure that keeps reconstructions and analyses reproducible while the map is still changing.
ocar.challenge: Users require immediate queries at arbitrary time points on up-to-petascale (~1 mm³) volumes. Prior tools (CATMAID, webKnossos, Eyewire, NeuTu) solved pieces of collaborative tracing or block-based proofreading, but not concurrent proofreading plus time-travel analysis at this scale.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald, Schneider-Mizell, and colleagues present CAVE in Nature Methods (2025): a suite of web services with distributed proofreading, continuous versioning via ChunkedGraph, and location-defined annotations that can be reassigned to segments at any time point, with schematized extensible annotation types.
ocar.resolution: CAVE is described as the only system that has successfully demonstrated proofreading of petascale connectomics datasets and is already used for many datasets, including the largest then available. An open API lets communities add lightweight services (NeuVue is cited as one example).
ocar.future_work: Scaling naively from MICrONS to ten-times-larger datasets would imply on the order of 10 trillion supervoxel edges, requiring further ChunkedGraph and SQL-annotation upgrades. The authors also note that expansion light-microscopy volumes will need similar infrastructure, and that deploying CAVE requires personnel who can manage container-based web services rather than standalone desktop tools.

summaries.beginner: When many people correct a giant brain map at once, cell names and synapse lists keep changing. CAVE is software that versions those edits so scientists can still run analyses and get the same answer later.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Methods (2025), this paper introduces CAVE, infrastructure for concurrent proofreading and reproducible analysis of up-to-petascale (~1 mm³) EM connectomes. A distributed proofreading system continuously versions large reconstructions, and annotations are defined by locations so they can be assigned to the current segment. That design enables analysis queries at arbitrary time points. The discussion places CAVE in a lineage from CATMAID, Eyewire, and NeuTu, and reports that it has demonstrated petascale proofreading. Engineering effort focused on cost-aware scaling, including ChunkedGraph v2.
summaries.advanced: CAVE is infrastructure, not a new segmentation algorithm. The ~1 mm³ figure is the targeted operating regime. Location-based annotations assume spatial coordinates remain meaningful across alignment versions. The 10-trillion-supervoxel figure is a naive scaling illustration from MICrONS, not a deployed dataset. Operational complexity (containerized web services) is an explicit adoption cost. Applicability to expansion light microscopy is prospective.

plain_language_summary: When many people correct a giant brain map at once, cell names and synapse lists keep changing. CAVE is software that versions those edits so scientists can still run analyses and get the same answer later.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian cortex contains diverse cell types whose anatomical, molecular, and functional properties are increasingly catalogued, but synaptic connectivity still determines how each type participates in the column.
ocar.challenge: Mapping connectivity rules at distinct-cell-type resolution remains difficult: it needs dense millimeter-scale EM plus classifications of inhibitory targeting and excitatory dendritic architecture.
ocar.action: Schneider-Mizell, Bodor, da Costa, and colleagues, in Nature (2025), used volumetric EM to census all inhibitory neurons among 1,352 densely segmented cells spanning all layers of mouse visual cortex, reconstructing more than 70,000 synapses, classifying inhibitory cells by dendritic-compartment targeting and excitatory cells from dendritic reconstructions with whole-cell synaptic-input maps.
ocar.resolution: Single-cell connectivity revealed a disinhibitory specialist that targets basket cells, widespread interneuron specificity for spatially intermingled excitatory subpopulations, and “motif groups” of diverse cells that collectively innervate both perisomatic and dendritic compartments of the same excitatory targets.
ocar.future_work: The principal limitation is generalizability: the data come from a single animal, one location near the edge of VISp, with at most a few examples per cell type, and from a narrow distance range. The authors argue companion analyses and agreement with functional SST connectivity measurements support broad results, but they call for measuring variability across cells, animals, and cortical locations, and for extending the analysis across a much wider extent to establish inhibitory motif groups more firmly.

summaries.beginner: Inhibitory cells in the cortex come in many kinds, but it has been unclear exactly whom each kind talks to. This team mapped inhibition across a column of mouse visual cortex and found that inhibitory cells are choosier than a random mix would suggest.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2025), Schneider-Mizell and colleagues present a synaptic-resolution census of inhibition across 1,352 densely segmented cells spanning all layers of mouse visual cortex, with more than 70,000 synapses. Inhibitory neurons were classified by dendritic-compartment targeting, and excitatory neurons by dendrites plus whole-cell synaptic-input maps. Results include a basket-cell-targeting disinhibitory specialist, widespread targeting specificity among intermingled excitatory subpopulations, and motif groups that jointly innervate soma and dendrites of the same excitatory cells. The work is framed as a foundation for linking multimodal neuronal atlases to cortical wiring.
summaries.advanced: The Limitations section is explicit: one animal, one VISp-edge location, few examples per type, and a limited volume that could bias connectivity if rules change with distance. Structural M-types are said to generally agree with morphology-only and morphoelectric-transcriptomic classifications, but this paper’s types are not themselves molecular. “Widespread specificity” is qualitative. The 2023 preprint reports the same cell and synapse counts, so this Nature paper is the journal version of that census.

plain_language_summary: Inhibitory cells in the cortex come in many kinds, but it has been unclear exactly whom each kind talks to. This team mapped inhibition across a column of mouse visual cortex and found that inhibitory cells are choosier than a random mix would suggest.

ocar.opportunity: Millimeter-scale EM volumes now yield dense cellular meshes with morphological detail from axon and dendrite branches down to spines, but turning those meshes into proofread neurons and usable features still takes heavy custom engineering.
ocar.challenge: Automated segmentation remains riddled with merge and split errors, and extracting spines, branches, and axonal–dendritic relations from elaborate 3D meshes is fragmented across tools.
ocar.action: Celii, Papadopoulos, Reimer, and colleagues introduce NEURD (Neural Decomposition) in Nature (2025): software that decomposes meshed neurons into compact, annotated graphs and uses those graphs to automate merge-error proofreading, cell classification, spine detection, axonal–dendritic proximities, and related annotations.
ocar.resolution: Built on existing open-source mesh software, NEURD is reported to reach state-of-the-art automated proofreading of merge errors and to make morphology and connectivity analyses more accessible on massive EM datasets. Code, documentation, and tutorials are released; some convenience products such as synapse spine labels and cell-type subclasses are available through CAVE.
ocar.future_work: The package is public with tutorials to reproduce pipeline stages on demand. Applying the same graph features uniformly across species and labs, and extending automation from merge errors to remaining split errors, would test how far the representation transfers.

summaries.beginner: Computers can now outline cells in huge electron-microscope volumes, but the outlines still have mistakes and are hard to measure. NEURD turns each cell’s 3D shape into a simpler labeled graph so corrections and measurements can be automated.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2025), Celii and colleagues present NEURD, which decomposes neuronal meshes from high-resolution EM volumes into feature-rich graphs. Those graphs automate merge-error proofreading, cell classification, spine detection, axonal–dendritic proximities, and related annotations. The authors report state-of-the-art automated merge-error proofreading and argue that the representation unlocks downstream morphological and connectivity analyses on millimetre-scale EM connectomes. Implementation details in the extract emphasize public code (github.com/reimerlab/NEURD) and CAVE-hosted convenience products.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract captured author contributions and code availability rather than a full Discussion, so quantitative proofreading benchmarks are not in the excerpt. NEURD targets merge errors specifically; split errors remain a general proofreading problem. The method operates on already-meshed, already-segmented neurons and inherits upstream failures. “State-of-the-art” is claimed without numeric scores here. MICrONS-associated authors and acknowledgements indicate the motivating volume family.

plain_language_summary: Computers can now outline cells in huge electron-microscope volumes, but the outlines still have mistakes and are hard to measure. NEURD turns each cell’s 3D shape into a simpler labeled graph so corrections and measurements can be automated.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic-resolution connectomics aims to map how evolution and individual experience implement circuits across the animal kingdom, but until recently accessible volumes were limited to specialized miniature neuropils.
ocar.challenge: Scaling 3D electron microscopy and analysis from about 100 µm³ to about 1 mm³ still leaves centimetre-scale targets—local circuits of larger brains including human, and whole-brain maps of small reptiles, rodents, birds, and non-human primates—out of reach, with remaining bottlenecks in tissue preparation, ablation or sectioning, imaging, and AI-based 3D analysis.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter reviews in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2025) two decades of methodological advances that expanded connectomically accessible synaptic-resolution volumes by a factor of about 1,000, discussing critical innovations alongside remaining challenges, in particular for centimetre-scale circuits such as a whole adult mouse brain.
ocar.resolution: The field can now move beyond miniature circuits to a large range of local mouse neuropil, including areas of cortical grey matter. The same advances also enable multifold mapping of comparably smaller circuits for connectomic screening of evolutionary determinism, individual experience, behavioural performance, and age-dependent or pathological alterations.
ocar.future_work: Resolving local cortical circuits of larger brains, including human, and whole-brain synaptic connectomes of small reptiles, rodents, birds, and non-human primates is identified as the next major target, with a whole adult mouse brain highlighted as a particular remaining challenge.

summaries.beginner: Scientists can now map tiny pieces of brain at the level of individual connections, about a thousand times larger than twenty years ago. This review explains what that makes possible next—and why a whole mouse brain at that detail is still a huge leap.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2025), Helmstaedter surveys synaptic-resolution connectomics and the methods that expanded accessible volumes from about 100 µm³ to about 1 mm³. He argues the field can now map a wide range of local mouse neuropil, including cortical grey matter, rather than only specialized miniature circuits. Remaining challenges for centimetre-scale targets such as a whole adult mouse brain are discussed across preparation, sectioning or ablation, imaging, and AI reconstruction. The same methods now allow repeated mapping of smaller circuits—“connectomic screening”—to study experience, aging, and pathology.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective review, not a new dataset; volume factors (about 1,000-fold; 100 µm³ to 1 mm³) are field-level estimates. Claims about readiness for local mouse cortex versus unreadiness for a whole mouse brain are strategic. “Connectomic screening” is a proposed use of smaller multifold maps. This review’s horizon includes human and other vertebrates even though mouse local neuropil is the near-term operating range.

plain_language_summary: Scientists can now map tiny pieces of brain at the level of individual connections, about a thousand times larger than twenty years ago. This review explains what that makes possible next—and why a whole mouse brain at that detail is still a huge leap.

ocar.opportunity: Most odors in Drosophila are encoded combinatorially across glomeruli, but some ecologically special odors use a single specialized pathway. Comparing dense glomerular connectomes can show how those computational styles differ at synaptic resolution.
ocar.challenge: Targeting identified glomeruli in volume EM, then scoring innervation, synapse composition, and motifs, is hard at the small scale of fly glomeruli. Reconstructing only the branded volume also prevents tracing neurons back to their somata, so individual identities used in whole-brain connectomes cannot be assigned.
ocar.action: Gruber, Cantera, Pleijzier, Hansson, Rybak and colleagues, in eLife (2025), combined transgenic labeling with near-infrared laser branding and FIB-SEM to densely reconstruct broadly tuned glomerulus DL5 and narrowly tuned DA2, then compared them with previously mapped narrow glomerulus VA1v.
ocar.resolution: Narrow glomeruli shared putative generic features: higher fiber and synapse density, lower OSN lateralization, stronger OSN axo-axonic connections, dendro-dendritic connections among many uniglomerular projection neurons, and less presynaptic input onto OSN axons. The single DL5 uPN also contained substantial autapses linking distant dendritic regions. Six shared circuit features of DA2 and VA1v versus DL5 are summarized as candidate adaptations of dedicated glomerular circuits.
ocar.future_work: The authors state that future studies analyzing precise synapse numbers across more individuals are needed to assess intra- and inter-animal variability, and that combining anatomy with physiology and computational modeling is essential to evaluate functional relevance. The limited scanned volume that blocked soma-based identification is an explicit drawback of the workflow.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies smell some odors with many glomeruli at once and other special odors with just one. This paper compares the wiring inside one “generalist” and one “specialist” glomerulus and lists connection patterns that may go with each job.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2025), Gruber and colleagues use laser branding plus FIB-SEM to reconstruct Drosophila glomeruli DL5 (broadly tuned) and DA2 (narrowly tuned) and compare them with previously mapped VA1v. They report differences among olfactory sensory neurons, uniglomerular projection neurons, and multiglomerular neurons, including higher innervation and synapse density in DA2. Narrow glomeruli showed less OSN lateralization, stronger OSN axo-axonic synapses, uPN dendro-dendritic coupling, and less presynaptic input on OSN axons. DL5’s single uPN contained many autapses spanning its dendritic tree. An eLife assessment notes the technical need to group local interneurons, centrifugal neurons, and multiglomerular projection neurons as “multiglomerular neurons.”
summaries.advanced: Generic features of narrow glomeruli are inferred from DA2 plus one previously mapped glomerulus (VA1v). DL5 autapses are from one uniglomerular PN. Soma-less reconstructions forced grouping of heterogeneous MGN classes, a caveat highlighted by reviewers. Motifs are anatomical; computational demands are interpreted from known glomerular tuning. Laser branding enables targeting but the extract does not quantify possible ultrastructural side effects.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies smell some odors with many glomeruli at once and other special odors with just one. This paper compares the wiring inside one “generalist” and one “specialist” glomerulus and lists connection patterns that may go with each job.

ocar.opportunity: Nervous systems coordinate effectors across the body during movement, but cellular-level synaptic circuits for whole-body control have been mapped in very few animals. A complete map of a segmented larva would show how senses reach muscles, cilia, glands, and pigment cells together.
ocar.challenge: Whole-animal synaptic connectomes had been described only for C. elegans and the Ciona tadpole larva. Reconstructing every neuronal and non-neuronal cell in a Platynereis whole-body EM volume, then classifying types and tracing left–right, intersegmental, and effector pathways, is a large annotation problem. Three-day-old larvae also lack later-developing appendages, crawling, feeding, and an enteric nervous system.
ocar.action: Verasztó, Jasek, Jékely and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2025), reconstruct and annotate the whole-body connectome of a three-day-old (early nectochaete) Platynereis dumerilii larva, mapping 9,162 cells into 294 types (202 neuronal and 92 non-neuronal) and analyzing modularity, multisensory integration, and motor circuits.
ocar.resolution: They report segment-specific cell types (heteromery) alongside serially homologous types across head, trunk segments, and pygidium, plus descending and ascending pathways, peptidergic circuits, and a multimodal mechanosensory girdle. The nervous system is largely feed-forward but includes recurrent motifs such as a ciliomotor pacemaker. The musculature comprises 53 muscle cell types. Platynereis is presented as the third whole-body connectome, with an order of magnitude more neurons than the nematode and tunicate maps.
ocar.future_work: The connectome is used to generate circuit-level hypotheses, including further integration of eyespot and adult-eye photoreceptors onto INR interneurons. Mushroom-body circuitry is described as a parallel feed-forward architecture that may still mature, because mushroom bodies grow later. Physiological tests of predicted sensory cross-talk and effector pathways are the implied next step.

summaries.beginner: This team mapped the cells and connections of an entire young marine worm, not just its brain. The map shows how segments share cell types and how senses can reach muscles, cilia, and glands across the body.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2025), Verasztó and colleagues present a whole-body synaptic connectome of a segmented Platynereis dumerilii larva. They annotated 9,162 cells and 294 types, including 202 neuronal and 92 non-neuronal classes. Analyses cover modularity, multisensory integration, left–right and intersegmental connectivity, and motor circuits for ciliated cells, glands, pigment cells, and muscles. Segment-specific types demonstrate heteromery, while repeated types across head, trunk, and pygidium suggest serial homology. Discussion emphasizes feed-forward sensory-to-effector flow with recurrent pockets, 53 muscle cell types, and a still-immature mushroom body.
summaries.advanced: Counts are annotation products of one three-day-old larva; stereotypy across individuals is not reported here. “Over 9,000” cells includes non-neuronal cells. Missing palps, crawling, and enteric systems are expected at this dispersing, non-feeding stage. Weak mushroom-body feedback may be a developmental snapshot. Functional predictions (for example photoreceptor convergence on INR cells) are hypotheses from anatomy.

plain_language_summary: This team mapped the cells and connections of an entire young marine worm, not just its brain. The map shows how segments share cell types and how senses can reach muscles, cilia, and glands across the body.

ocar.opportunity: Human brain function at synaptic resolution has been limited by scarce high-quality tissue and the difficulty of reconstructing a cubic millimeter at nanoscale. Surgical access-path cortex can supply a sample large enough to contain circuits spanning all six layers.
ocar.challenge: Human cortex is rarely biopsied except near pathology; organoids lack cortical layering; and capturing both nanometer synapses and a millimeter-scale volume requires more than a petabyte of serial-section EM plus intensive alignment, segmentation, and proofreading.
ocar.action: Shapson-Coe, Januszewski, Berger, Lichtman, Jain and colleagues, in Science (2024), imaged a 1 mm³ piece of human temporal cortex removed to access an epileptic focus, reconstructed cells, vessels, and synapses computationally, and released the 1.4-petabyte H01 resource with Neuroglancer, CREST, CAVE, and VAST.
ocar.resolution: The volume contains about 57,000 cells, about 230 mm of blood vessels, and about 150 million synapses. Glia outnumbered neurons 2:1, oligodendrocytes were the most common cell, deep-layer excitatory “compass” cells in layer 6 had basal dendrites oriented in two preferred directions, and rare powerful axonal inputs of 50 or more synapses sat among thousands of weak connections per neuron.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect many other novel phenomena in the still incompletely scrutinized volume and invite community proofreading. Studying additional rapidly preserved samples would address special challenges of human tissue, including membranous profiles sometimes seen after post-mortem delay.

summaries.beginner: Researchers reconstructed a cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex at very high detail and posted the data for anyone to explore. They found more support cells than neurons, and a few unusually strong connections mixed in with many weak ones.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2024), Shapson-Coe and colleagues present a nanoscale reconstruction of 1 mm³ of human temporal cortex obtained during surgery to reach an underlying lesion. Serial-section EM produced 1.4 petabytes containing about 57,000 cells, about 230 mm of blood vessels, and about 150 million synapses. Analysis found glia outnumbering neurons 2:1, oligodendrocytes as the most common cell, layer-6 compass cells with two preferred basal-dendrite directions, and rare multi-synaptic axonal inputs of 50 or more synapses. Shared tools include Neuroglancer, CREST pathway exploration, CAVE proofreading, and VAST annotation.
summaries.advanced: Tissue is surgical access-path cortex from a patient with epilepsy, so “normal human cortex” is an approximation. Automated reconstruction is incomplete. Up-to-50-synapse inputs and compass-cell orientations are described as previously unrecognized in this sample; prevalence across individuals is unknown. The discussion notes oddities in supplementary figures. Human samples can show empty membranous profiles not seen in rapidly preserved tissue; the authors state H01 quality was sufficient to identify synapses.

plain_language_summary: Researchers reconstructed a cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex at very high detail and posted the data for anyone to explore. They found more support cells than neurons, and a few unusually strong connections mixed in with many weak ones.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric reconstructions now yield neuron-level connectomes in fruit fly, mouse, and human, creating a chance to test whether those networks share simple physical and topological organizing rules.
ocar.challenge: Spatial embedding and degree sequence each explain part of the structure, but neither constraint alone recovers the other: neuron positions look distance-optimal, yet space misses the broad degree distribution, and degrees miss geometry.
ocar.action: Salova and Kovács, in Network Neuroscience (2024), construct contactomes (networks of neurons in physical contact) alongside connectomes and formulate scalable maximum-entropy models that incorporate both spatial or contact constraints and topological constraints.
ocar.resolution: Joint models captured biological and network characteristics beyond the input data, including synaptic weights and graphlet statistics, pointing to a simple set of shared organizing principles across the three organisms.
ocar.future_work: Testing whether the same joint spatial–topological ensemble predicts held-out volumes or developmental stages would show if the principles are generative rather than descriptive of current snapshots.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring is shaped both by which cells sit near each other and by how many partners each cell has. This paper shows you need both kinds of rules to copy the structure of fly, mouse, and human connection maps.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Network Neuroscience (2024), Salova and Kovács model fruit-fly, mouse, and human neural connectomes in physical context by constructing contactomes of neurons in contact. Neuron positions are highly optimal in distance to neighbors, but spatial constraints alone miss topology including the broad degree distribution, while the degree sequence alone misses spatial structure. Scalable maximum-entropy models combining both constraint types generate networks that also capture synaptic weights and graphlet statistics. The authors interpret this as a shared, simple set of organizing principles across organisms.
summaries.advanced: “Shared principles” are inferred from successful joint maximum-entropy fits, not from a single universal parameter set reported here. Contactomes depend on morphological reconstructions and contact definitions that may differ by dataset. Human and mouse reconstructions used here are local volumes, not whole brains, unlike the fly case.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring is shaped both by which cells sit near each other and by how many partners each cell has. This paper shows you need both kinds of rules to copy the structure of fly, mouse, and human connection maps.

ocar.opportunity: In insects the neck connective is a physical and informational bottleneck between brain and ventral nerve cord, so a complete account of descending, ascending, and sensory ascending neurons is needed to link sensation to action.
ocar.challenge: These neurons are split across brain and nerve-cord EM volumes and differ by sex, so they must be matched across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes and tied to genetic driver lines.
ocar.action: Stürner, Brooks, Jefferis, Eichler and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2024), integrate three EM datasets to proofread and match female Drosophila descending and ascending neurons, compare them with the male nerve cord, match 51% of descending cell types to light-level driver lines, and classify all ascending populations.
ocar.resolution: They describe architecture, tracts, neuropil innervation, and connectivity of neck-connective neurons, including chains of descending and ascending neurons spanning the neck that may subserve motor sequences, and a complete account of sexually dimorphic DN and AN populations implicated in female ovipositor extrusion (DNp13), male courtship (DNa12/aSP22), and song (AN hemilineage 08B). They frame this as the first EM-level circuit analyses spanning an adult animal’s entire central nervous system.
ocar.future_work: Completing driver-line matches beyond the reported 51% of DN types, and functional tests of the identified dimorphic circuits, would close the loop from EM identity to behavior.

summaries.beginner: Messages between a fly’s brain and its body travel through a narrow neck. This team finished mapping those up and down neurons in a female fly, compared them with a male, and tied many types to genetic tools.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Stürner and colleagues present a complete connectomic description of Drosophila ascending and descending neurons in the female nervous system, integrating three EM datasets and comparing them with the male nerve cord. Proofread reconstructions were matched across hemispheres, datasets, and sexes; 51% of descending cell types were matched to light-level driver lines, and all ascending populations were classified. The authors report neck-spanning DN–AN chains and sexually dimorphic populations, including circuits for ovipositor extrusion, male courtship, and song.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract captured the abstract and introduction plus the reference list rather than a dedicated discussion, so circuit interpretations follow the abstract. “Complete” refers to matched ascending/descending populations, not every neuron in brain plus VNC. Driver-line matching is 51% of DN types. Behavioral roles are assigned via implicated circuits and prior literature, not new behavior experiments in this extract. Sexual dimorphism analyses depend on cross-dataset matching between female and male nerve cords.

plain_language_summary: Messages between a fly’s brain and its body travel through a narrow neck. This team finished mapping those up and down neurons in a female fly, compared them with a male, and tied many types to genetic tools.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian whole-brain connectomes are a foundational planning target: mouse volumes may soon come within reach, while human volumes remain more distant. Groups organizing those projects need a quantitative comparison of imaging methods that can resolve all synapses at relevant speed.
ocar.challenge: The Drosophila brain is only 0.0175 mm³ versus about 500 mm³ for mouse and about 1,200,000 mm³ for human, so throughput must rise dramatically. Distinct methods involve different technical challenges, and some extrapolation is required for emerging pipelines that are not yet fully tested.
ocar.action: Collins, Huffman, and Koene, in Cell Reports Methods (2024), quantitatively compare electron microscopy techniques and expansion light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (ExLSFM), restricting attention to methods with synapse-identifying resolution and mammalian-brain-relevant speed, with calculation details in supplemental information.
ocar.resolution: Under a $100M instrument budget they estimate mouse-brain imaging at 0.69 years with 200 bdTEM systems (3.6×3.6×45 nm voxels) versus 0.014 years with 333 VIPS ExLLSM systems (effective 12.4×12.4×30 nm). Human-brain estimates are 1,667 years versus 34 years under the same budgets. Raw mouse data storage is given as about 85.7 petabytes; human as about 205.7 exabytes. EM is judged the most reliable near-term path; ExLSFM is faster and molecularly multiplexable but still early.
ocar.future_work: The authors argue that developing multiple modalities in parallel is likely best. Mapping the human connectome may still require paradigm-shifting advances such as synchrotron X-ray nanotomography and/or massive parallelization. They also note there is currently no method for properly sectioning pre- or post-expansion tissues at whole-brain scale.

summaries.beginner: Scientists want maps of entire mammal brains at the level of connections, starting with the mouse. This paper compares electron microscopes and expansion light-sheet methods to see which could finish that job, and on what timescale.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Cell Reports Methods (2024), Collins, Huffman, and Koene compare imaging technologies for whole-brain mammalian connectomics. Mouse brain volume is given as about 28,571 times Drosophila; human about 2,400 times mouse. Tabled estimates for a $100M fleet put mouse EM acquisition at under a year and ExLSFM much faster, while human EM remains millennial-scale and ExLSFM multi-decadal. Sample-preparation estimates include 200 ATUMs sectioning a mouse brain in 1.74 days versus 11.42 years for human. The discussion treats EM as the mature pipeline and ExLSFM as an emerging speed-and-molecular alternative.
summaries.advanced: This is a prospective comparison, not an empirical bake-off on one sample. Times assume stated instrument counts, voxel sizes, and linear scaling. Expansion light-sheet still lacks a high-throughput connectomics pipeline in this account. Storage-cost figures are order-of-magnitude planning numbers. Human whole-brain synaptic imaging remains aspirational; synchrotron X-ray is mentioned as a possible future enabler, not a present solution.

plain_language_summary: Scientists want maps of entire mammal brains at the level of connections, starting with the mouse. This paper compares electron microscopes and expansion light-sheet methods to see which could finish that job, and on what timescale.

ocar.opportunity: A deep understanding of how the brain controls behaviour requires mapping neural circuits down to the muscles they control. In flies those motor neurons live in the ventral nerve cord, analogous to the vertebrate spinal cord, and a synapse-level motor wiring diagram for a limbed animal had been lacking.
ocar.challenge: A dense EM volume of an adult female Drosophila VNC still needs automated neuron and synapse segmentation plus an atlas of which motor neurons innervate which muscles. Interpreting the wiring also requires guessing excitatory versus inhibitory identity.
ocar.action: Azevedo, Lesser, Phelps, Mark, Lee, Tuthill and colleagues, in Nature (2024), apply automated tools to segment neurons and identify synapses in a female fly VNC EM dataset (FANC), and map leg and wing motor-neuron muscle targets with genetic driver lines and X-ray holographic nanotomography.
ocar.resolution: They report roughly 45 million synapses and 14,600 neuronal cell bodies, a motor-neuron atlas, and circuits coordinating leg and wing movements during take-off. Reconstruction revealed independent control of femur and trochanter segments previously thought to be mechanically fused. At publication the community had proofread roughly half of FANC; automated reconstruction and CAVE tools already enabled interactive inquiry.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that multiple VNC connectomes will enable comparison across individuals and identification of sexually dimorphic circuits. Remaining challenges include assigning synapse sign; they use hemilineage identity as a candidate neurotransmitter proxy, as in the escape circuitry. Matching VNC neurons to GAL4 lines is presented as the route to in vivo tests.

summaries.beginner: A fruit fly’s “spinal cord” contains the cells that move legs and wings. This team automatically traced that cord, matched motor neurons to muscles, and spotted circuits that help the fly take off.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2024), Azevedo and colleagues present an automated dense reconstruction of an adult female Drosophila ventral nerve cord. The VNC contains roughly 45 million synapses and 14,600 neuronal cell bodies. Muscle targets of leg and wing motor neurons were mapped with genetic driver lines and X-ray holographic nanotomography, yielding a motor-neuron atlas used to identify take-off coordination circuits. Discussion emphasizes ongoing community proofreading (about half complete at publication), comparison with the male VNC, and the finding of independent femur and trochanter control.
summaries.advanced: Counts are for one female VNC. Automated segmentation plus targeted motor-neuron mapping is not fully proofread completeness. Take-off circuit identification uses the atlas and connectivity; the extract does not report new behavioral recordings. Hemilineage-based transmitter assignment is a candidate, not a direct measurement. XNH complements EM for muscle targeting rather than replacing synaptic EM.

plain_language_summary: A fruit fly’s “spinal cord” contains the cells that move legs and wings. This team automatically traced that cord, matched motor neurons to muscles, and spotted circuits that help the fly take off.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans synaptic connectome is fully mapped, but much less is known about the causal signaling network that actually propagates activity. Relating those two lenses on the same nervous system is a central structure–function question.
ocar.challenge: Because anatomy describes direct wired contacts while signaling captures multi-hop flow, feedback, neuromodulation, and extrasynaptic effects, network features need not be preserved across the two descriptions. It is even unclear whether high anatomical out-degree implies strong or diluted signaling impact.
ocar.action: Dvali, Seguin, Betzel, and Leifer, in PRX Life (2024), compare the modular architecture of a C. elegans signal-propagation network measured with calcium imaging and optogenetics to anatomical wiring from electron microscopy, including rich-club analyses of both graphs.
ocar.resolution: Signaling modules were not aligned with anatomical module boundaries, yet the pharynx remained a separate community in both. Signaling modules were enriched for specific cell types and functions. A signaling rich club of hub neurons differed in membership from the anatomical rich club, overlapping only at AVEL/R, which have some of the highest anatomical degrees. Bilaterally symmetric neurons were much more likely to share communities in anatomy (38 times) than in signaling (twice).
ocar.future_work: The authors conclude that perhaps only the most pronounced network features should be expected to survive across signaling and anatomy. They point to network models that consider synaptic dilution, and to contributions from neuromodulation, extrasynaptic signaling, and gene expression, as avenues for explaining the remaining divergence.

summaries.beginner: Knowing which worm neurons are wired together is not the same as knowing which ones actually pass signals. This study measures signal spread and finds that the functional groups only partly match the wiring groups.
summaries.intermediate: Published in PRX Life (2024), Dvali and colleagues compare the C. elegans synaptic connectome with a causal signal-propagation network from calcium imaging and optogenetics. Signaling modules do not align with anatomical module boundaries, although the pharynx is a separate community in both maps. Signaling modules are enriched for particular cell types and functions, and a rich club of signaling hubs has different membership from the anatomical rich club, overlapping only at AVEL/R. Discussion emphasizes that anatomy is monosynaptic while signaling is poly-synaptic, which can explain weaker bilateral community coupling in the functional graph.
summaries.advanced: The signaling network is defined by this perturbation-and-imaging assay; different stimuli or timescales could regroup modules. Only extreme anatomical features (pharynx; AVEL/R) are clearly preserved. The 38-times versus twice bilateral-community figures are specific to this community detection. Rich-club comparison depends on thresholding both graphs. Dilution models and neuromodulation are proposed explanations, not fitted here.

plain_language_summary: Knowing which worm neurons are wired together is not the same as knowing which ones actually pass signals. This study measures signal spread and finds that the functional groups only partly match the wiring groups.

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila mushroom body is the center for associative learning, and split-GAL4 drivers plus EM connectomes already support precise interrogation of its core cells. Many cell types upstream and downstream still lacked specific genetic access.
ocar.challenge: Without driver lines, functional tests of sugar sensory neurons, putative nociceptive ascending neurons, olfactory and thermo-/hygro-sensory projection neurons, and interneurons connected to mushroom-body extrinsic cells stall even when the wiring is known.
ocar.action: Shuai, Aso, and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2024), describe a collection of over 800 split-GAL4 and split-LexA drivers covering approximately 300 cell types, characterize activation phenotypes for a subset, and use associated confocal images to quantify morphological stereotypy.
ocar.resolution: They identify a sugar sensory neuron line most suitable for reward substitution and find that MBON08/MBON09 exhibit striking individuality and left–right asymmetry across animals. Together with EM connectome maps, the collection is offered as a resource for functional dissection of adult associative-learning circuits.
ocar.future_work: Systematic functional use of the new lines, especially the less-stereotyped MBONs, is needed to test how individual morphological variation affects learning. Conversion examples of split-LexA reagents are shown as a route to intersectional experiments.

summaries.beginner: To test what each cell type does in fly learning, scientists need genetic on-switches for those cells. This paper releases hundreds of such switches and notices that one pair of output cells looks surprisingly different from fly to fly.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Shuai and colleagues present over 800 split-GAL4 and split-LexA drivers covering approximately 300 Drosophila cell types, including sugar sensory neurons, putative nociceptive ascending neurons, olfactory and thermo-/hygro-sensory projection neurons, and interneurons connected with mushroom-body extrinsic neurons. Activation phenotyping identified a sugar sensory line suited to reward substitution. Confocal analysis showed MBON08/MBON09 individuality and asymmetry. The introduction frames the mushroom body as about 2,000 Kenyon cells and 15 DAN/MBON compartments whose synaptic weights store memories.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract captured figure supplements on MBON08/09 rather than a prose Discussion, so future-work statements are inferred from the resource framing. Coverage is “approximately 300 cell types” among “over 800” drivers; per-type specificity is not quantified here. MBON individuality is morphological from light microscopy, not a connectivity measurement in this extract. Driver utility depends on split-half expression not detailed in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: To test what each cell type does in fly learning, scientists need genetic on-switches for those cells. This paper releases hundreds of such switches and notices that one pair of output cells looks surprisingly different from fly to fly.

ocar.opportunity: Accurate neuron segmentation is essential for automated connectome reconstruction, but image-based convolutional nets are limited to local shape context. Human proofreaders instead judge global 3D neuron renderings that can span up to 10^12 voxels.
ocar.challenge: Scaling from fly to mouse (about 500 times larger) would require orders of magnitude more manual effort with current technology. Existing local CNNs can achieve error-free paths up to 1.1 mm, yet the fruit fly brain still contains about 145 meters of wiring that needs proofreading.
ocar.action: Troidl, Knittel, Li, Zhan, Pfister, and Turaga, on bioRxiv (2024), introduce a point affinity transformer that embeds a (multi-)neuron point cloud into a fixed-length feature set from which any point-pair affinity can be decoded, supporting clustering for automatic proofreading and mapping features into a contrastive space for type classification.
ocar.resolution: Evaluated on three benchmark datasets derived from state-of-the-art connectomes, the method outperformed point transformers, graph neural networks, and unsupervised clustering baselines on segmentation-error correction and neuron-type classification.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose augmenting point clouds with local image features (for example SegCLR or synapse type), using embeddings from sparse labels in one region or species for unsupervised type discovery in others, extending proofreading to light-microscopic point clouds from simple thresholding, and training decoders for skeletons and Gaussian-splat renderings from sparse samples.

summaries.beginner: Computers that trace neurons usually look at small patches of the image. This method looks at the whole sketched shape of a cell as a cloud of points, which helps it fix tracing mistakes and guess the cell’s type.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Troidl and colleagues present a point affinity transformer for global neuron-shape reasoning. A (multi-)neuron point cloud is embedded into a fixed-length feature set from which point-pair affinities can be decoded, enabling clustering for automatic proofreading. The same features map into a contrastive space used for neuron-type classification. The introduction motivates the work with FlyWire-scale manual effort and the 145 meters of fly-brain wiring still requiring proofreading. On three connectome-derived benchmarks the approach outperformed point transformers, GNNs, and unsupervised clustering.
summaries.advanced: Outperformance is reported without numeric scores in the extract. Benchmarks derived from existing connectomes may not capture the full error distribution of raw automated segmentation. The method assumes a point-cloud representation, which already requires a skeleton or mesh step. Cited FlyWire labor figures (622 researchers; 33 human-years) describe community proofreading scale; they should not be read as a new measurement in this methods paper.

plain_language_summary: Computers that trace neurons usually look at small patches of the image. This method looks at the whole sketched shape of a cell as a cloud of points, which helps it fix tracing mistakes and guess the cell’s type.

ocar.opportunity: Neuron-resolution connectomes with cell-type annotations, such as the larval Drosophila brain, finally let researchers test whether graph communities defined from connectivity alone correspond to biological cell classes.
ocar.challenge: This kind of annotation comparison is common at meso- and macro-scale but rarer at nano-scale. Standard community detection is often single-scale; relating multi-level blocks to function, cell type, and communication paths is harder.
ocar.action: Betzel, Puxeddu, and Seguin, on bioRxiv (2024), apply a hierarchical weighted stochastic blockmodel to a published larval Drosophila connectome and compare blocks to functional and cell-type maps, then examine assortativity, rich-club membership, and polysynaptic trajectories.
ocar.resolution: Communities largely partitioned neurons by function and cell type and mostly interacted assortatively, reflecting functional segregation. A minority of non-assortative communities formed a rich club composed mostly of interneurons that receive sensory/ascending inputs and deliver descending outputs, and those interneurons mediated communication across modules and hierarchical scales.
ocar.future_work: The authors frame the study as a step toward bridging complex-systems and neurobiological investigation. Whether the same hierarchical block structure appears in adult fly or other nano-scale connectomes would test if the larva’s mixed assortative/rich-club architecture is general.

summaries.beginner: This paper groups larval fruit-fly neurons into nested communities using only the wiring, then checks those groups against known cell types. Most groups stay among similar cells, but a small hub club of in-between cells helps messages travel across the brain.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Betzel, Puxeddu, and Seguin apply a hierarchical weighted stochastic blockmodel to the larval Drosophila connectome. Detected communities partition neurons by function and cell type and mostly interact assortatively. A small set of communities interact non-assortatively; their neurons form a rich club of interneurons bridging sensory/ascending input to descending output. Polysynaptic signaling is described as following specific trajectories across the hierarchy. Supplementary comparisons in the extract contrast the blockmodel with modularity maximization (203 versus 1,070 communities) and repeat annotation-enrichment analyses.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract captured supplementary figures rather than a prose Discussion. Community labels are model-based; alternative algorithms shift counts and boundaries. Assortativity is the majority pattern, so the rich-club interneuron story concerns a minority of blocks. Communication trajectories are inferred from topology, not measured activity. Enrichment relative to eight level-two communities depends on those annotation maps.

plain_language_summary: This paper groups larval fruit-fly neurons into nested communities using only the wiring, then checks those groups against known cell types. Most groups stay among similar cells, but a small hub club of in-between cells helps messages travel across the brain.

ocar.opportunity: The first whole-brain connectome of an adult fly, with over 130,000 neurons and millions of synaptic connections, makes brain-wide network statistics tractable rather than regional. Motifs, hubs, and neuropil subnetworks can now be compared with other animals and with cell-type and neurotransmitter annotations.
ocar.challenge: Anatomy suggests bottlenecks: only 12% of neurons cross hemispheres and 6% cross between the central brain and optic lobes, yet the brain remains robustly interconnected with short path lengths. Interpreting those statistics requires combining wiring with predicted transmitters and types.
ocar.action: Lin, Yang, Dorkenwald, Murthy and colleagues, in Nature (2024), compute two- and three-node motif prevalence and strength in the FlyWire whole-brain network, relate metrics to neurotransmitter composition and cell types, analyze rich-club organization, and examine 78 neuropil subnetworks, sharing products in FlyWire Codex.
ocar.resolution: The fly brain is highly recurrent and shows rich-club organization, with a large population (30% of the connectome) of highly connected neurons. Subsets of rich-club neurons are proposed as integrators or broadcasters. Relative to average neurons, rich-club cells are more likely to synapse in both hemispheres and to connect optic lobes to the central brain, which the authors suggest keeps path lengths short across anatomical bottlenecks.
ocar.future_work: The authors expect ascending and descending neurons to join a central-nervous-system rich club once a complete CNS connectome exists, and they present the statistics as a baseline for comparison to other Drosophila individuals and other species. Future functional experiments focused on the rich-club population are proposed to test whether those neurons shorten functional path lengths as they do anatomical ones.

summaries.beginner: With a whole fruit-fly brain wiring diagram in hand, this paper counts common connection patterns and finds a large club of well-connected cells. About three in ten neurons sit in that highly connected group.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2024), Lin and colleagues compute network statistics on the FlyWire whole-brain Drosophila connectome. They quantify two- and three-node motifs, relate them to neurotransmitter and cell-type annotations, and compare metrics with other animals. They report rich-club organization involving about 30% of neurons and identify candidate integrator and broadcaster subsets. Subnetwork analyses cover 78 neuropils. Discussion notes that despite left–right and central-brain/optic-lobe bottlenecks, rich-club neurons’ broad spatial reach may explain short path lengths.
summaries.advanced: A rich club containing 30% of neurons is unusually large; membership depends on degree thresholds not specified in the extract. Neurotransmitter predictions (acetylcholine, GABA, glutamate, dopamine, serotonin, octopamine) enhance interpretation but are predictions. Motif profiles can differ by neuropil: the gnathal ganglion is cited as having similar three-node motifs but much lower reciprocity. Statistics inherit FlyWire proofreading error. Integrator/broadcaster roles are anatomical hypotheses.

plain_language_summary: With a whole fruit-fly brain wiring diagram in hand, this paper counts common connection patterns and finds a large club of well-connected cells. About three in ten neurons sit in that highly connected group.

ocar.opportunity: Local EM reconstructions inform regional circuits but are inadequate for brain-wide function. A whole adult brain wiring diagram with interoperable annotations would let researchers trace pathways from sensors to motor, endocrine, and descending outputs across both hemispheres and between central brain and optic lobes.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing chemical synapses among more than a hundred thousand neurons, then annotating classes, types, nerves, hemilineages, and predicted transmitters, is a community-scale proofreading and software problem. Earlier hemibrain coverage omitted most of the optic lobes and the subesophageal zone and lacked both sides of the brain.
ocar.action: Dorkenwald, Matsliah, Seung, Murthy, the FlyWire Consortium and colleagues, in Nature (2024), present a neuronal wiring diagram of an adult female Drosophila with 5×10⁷ chemical synapses among 139,255 neurons, plus annotations and data products for download, programmatic access, and interactive browsing.
ocar.resolution: They derive a projectome of inter-region projections, trace information flow from sensory and ascending inputs to motor, endocrine, and descending outputs, and illustrate structure-to-behavior analysis by tracing from a subset of photoreceptors (including ocelli) to descending motor pathways. Proofreading used an estimated 33 person-years, compared with 50 person-years for the partial hemibrain, with similar reported accuracy. The open ecosystem is offered as a template for other species.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that a connectome in the strictest sense might also include the ventral nerve cord. Twig-to-backbone attachment currently limits synaptic completeness: raising the postsynaptic attachment rate from 44.7% to 50% would require proofreading more than 700,000 additional fragments, so further gains depend on imaging, alignment, and automated reconstruction. Electrical synapses are not included. Observed synapse counts underrepresent true numbers, and some weak connections remain undetected, though connections with more than nine synapses are nearly all detected.

summaries.beginner: This paper releases a wiring diagram of an entire adult fruit-fly brain: which cells connect, what kinds they are, and roughly what chemical they use. The map is public so others can follow paths from the eyes to the cells that drive movement.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2024), FlyWire presents a whole-brain wiring diagram of an adult female Drosophila melanogaster containing 5×10⁷ chemical synapses between 139,255 neurons, with annotations of cell classes and types, nerves, hemilineages, and predicted neurotransmitters. The authors derive a projectome, analyze information flow from inputs to outputs across hemispheres and between central brain and optic lobes, and trace photoreceptor-to-descending pathways as a circuit example. Discussion contrasts FlyWire’s ssTEM-plus-boundary-net stack with hemibrain FIB-SEM and flood-filling nets, and reports 33 person-years of proofreading.
summaries.advanced: Neuron and synapse counts are reconstruction products of one female brain and will shift with further proofreading. Neurotransmitter identities are predictions. Incomplete twig attachment is the main accuracy limit; the 44.7% postsynaptic attachment rate is an explicit caveat. Pathway tracing from a photoreceptor subset is illustrative. Companion papers (annotation, network statistics, effectome) should be read alongside this resource paper.

plain_language_summary: This paper releases a wiring diagram of an entire adult fruit-fly brain: which cells connect, what kinds they are, and roughly what chemical they use. The map is public so others can follow paths from the eyes to the cells that drive movement.

ocar.opportunity: A long-standing goal is to read circuit function from form. In many vertebrate regions connectivity is highly recurrent without obvious topography, so it has been unclear how neural coding emerges from wiring. The larval zebrafish hindbrain gaze-control network, including the oculomotor neural integrator, is a concrete test case.
ocar.challenge: Dense synaptic reconstructions must be turned into modules and dynamics that can be compared with cellular-resolution activity, not just described anatomically. Persistent eye-position activity is thought to require low-dimensional attractor dynamics supported by positive feedback, which had not been shown as an anatomical cycle structure in this circuit.
ocar.action: Vishwanathan, Sood, Goldman, Aksay, Seung and colleagues, in Nature Neuroscience (2024), reconstruct a synaptic wiring diagram of the larval zebrafish brainstem, identify strongly connected modules, and build a neural-network model directly from that diagram to predict eye-position coding and dynamics, then compare predictions with calcium imaging.
ocar.resolution: Modules were specialized for eye versus body movements. The eye-movement module contained two three-block cycles consistent with the positive feedback long hypothesized for oculomotor attractors. Model predictions for cellular-resolution coding of eye position and neural dynamics were statistically verified with calcium imaging.
ocar.future_work: Data, skeletons, and synapses are released, with modularity analyses and network simulations available as code. Applying the same connectome-to-model-to-physiology loop to other vertebrate motor modules would test whether cycle motifs generalize beyond this oculomotor example.

summaries.beginner: Researchers mapped connections in a young zebrafish’s brainstem, then asked whether the wiring could predict how cells encode eye position. The predictions matched calcium-imaging measurements.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Neuroscience (2024), Vishwanathan and colleagues reconstruct a synaptic wiring diagram of the larval zebrafish brainstem and use it to predict function. Strongly connected modules turned out to be specialized for eye versus body movements, and the eye-movement module contained two three-block cycles that can support hypothesized low-dimensional oculomotor attractors. A network model built directly from the wiring diagram predicted cellular-resolution eye-position coding and neural dynamics, and those predictions were statistically verified with calcium imaging. The work is presented as a demonstration of connectome-based brain modeling, contrasting with topographic fly navigation and early visual systems.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract captured data/code availability rather than a full Discussion.
